extraction.name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and instance segmentation in complex everyday scenes, containing 91 common object categories, 2.5 million labeled instances, and 328,000 images, with annotations collected via crowd workers.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin; Michael Maire; Serge Belongie; Lubomir Bourdev; Ross Girshick; James Hays; Pietro Perona; Deva Ramanan; C. Lawrence Zitnick; Piotr Dollar
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were collected primarily from Flickr using object-object and object-scene search queries to find non-iconic images with contextual relationships. The dataset was then annotated through a multi-stage Amazon Mechanical Turk pipeline for category labeling, instance spotting, instance segmentation, verification, and captions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: User-generated content data, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consisted of candidate images collected from Flickr via searches for pairs of object categories and object-scene category pairs, with additional single-category searches followed by filtering when needed.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize duplicates across train/validation/test splits. Bounding boxes for experiments were derived from segmentation masks.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Candidate images were filtered to remove invalid or iconic images. For some categories, single-category searches were used with explicit filtering. Near-duplicates were removed before dataset splitting.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotation used a three-stage AMT pipeline: hierarchical category labeling, instance spotting, and instance segmentation, followed by segmentation verification. Eight workers labeled each image for category presence and instance spotting; one worker segmented each instance after category-specific training; 3 to 5 workers verified each segmentation. Five captions were also added per image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors analyzed annotation quality by comparing AMT workers to expert annotators, emphasizing recall for category labeling. Ground truth was based on expert majority vote. They found the union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any expert, estimated over 99% recall for object categories not later rejected as false positives, and used verification voting thresholds to discard poor segmentations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 8 for category labeling; 8 for instance spotting; 1 for instance segmentation with 3 to 5 verification judgments; 5 captions per image
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers; expert annotators included seven co-authors of the paper; children aged 4 to 8 were consulted for category elicitation.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset was released in stages, with the first half in 2014 and the second half in 2015. Train and validation annotations are released, but test annotations are withheld for evaluation server use. The dataset is intended to evolve and grow over time, with up-to-date information online and possible future addition of segmentations for omitted categories.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive advancement of object detection and segmentation algorithms and support future annotations such as scene types, attributes, and sentence descriptions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset intentionally emphasizes non-iconic images and contextual scenes rather than iconic object-centric images. Category presence can be ambiguous, and some categories were excluded or limited due to ambiguity, difficulty, too many instances, confusion with other categories, or too few instances.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently labels only 'thing' categories, not 'stuff'. The 2014 release includes segmentation masks for only 80 of 91 categories, with 11 categories omitted due to annotation difficulty, ambiguity, confusion, too many instances, or too few instances. In dense scenes, only 10-15 instances per category are individually segmented and the rest are marked as crowds and ignored during evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for object detection and instance segmentation in natural scenes; benchmarking scene understanding and contextual reasoning; evaluation via released train/validation annotations and withheld test annotations through an evaluation server.

name.evidence: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context

description.evidence: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Our dataset contains photos of 91 objects types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old. With a total of 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images...

rai:dataCollection.evidence: To create a large-scale dataset that accomplishes these three goals we employed a novel pipeline for gathering data with extensive use of Amazon Mechanical Turk. First and most importantly, we harvested a large set of images containing contextual relationships and noniconic object views. We accomplished this using a surprisingly simple yet effective technique that queries for pairs of objects in conjunction with images retrieved via scene-based queries [17], [3]. Next, each image was labeled as containing particular object categories using a hierarchical labeling approach [18]. For each category found, the individual instances were labeled, verified, and finally segmented.
